newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Ecuador oil investors wait on pipeline expansion.
newsitem.headline: Ecuador oil investors wait on pipeline expansion.

text.p: Ecuador has made progress on a plan to expand its main oil pipeline, a project that could add 85,000 barrels per day (bpd) to the country's oil exports next year, analysts said on Wednesday.

However, the expansion would represent only a temporary solution to a long-standing transport problem which has been standing in the way of increased output from Latin America's second-largest oil exporter, analysts add.
The existing SOTE pipeline linking Ecuador's main oil producing region with the Pacific coast is the country's economic lifeline, used for 85 percent of the country's 390,000 bpd oil output.
Analysts say its limited capacity is currently restricting output by about 17 percent and, more importantly, is acting as a brake to foreign invesment in new exploration.

Sondra Scott, Cambridge Energy Research Associates' Mexico City-based Latin America analyst, said Ecuador needs to guarantee 600,000 bpd in pipeline capacity to realise its potential for production growth over the next 15 years.
"At the corporate level, there continues to be concern and there will be no rush in investment until this problem is solved," Scott said.
Ecuador's recent chaotic political history has produced several plans to solve the transport capacity crunch, but most have been abandoned or cancelled with each change of administration.
The latest plan is to increase the line's capacity from 325,000 bpd to 410,000 bpd in a modest upgrading project.
"It would solve the problem for 1998, but if we look at 1999 we already see 30,000-40,000 barrels per day of shut in capacity," Scott said.
PetroEcuador engaged Halliburton, a subsidiary of engineering group Brown and Root, for preliminary design of the scheme under a contract that had been cancelled by the previous Bucaram government.

The project involves replacing some tubing, installing new pumps and increasing storage and loading capacity at the export terminal. An Ecuadorean industry source said 34 companies had expressed an interest in participating.

But PetroEcuador has yet to work out funding for the plan. Four international oil companies signed a preliminary accord with PetroEcuador last Friday to investigate ways of obtaining the $120 million needed.
Occidental, Arco, YPF and City Investing had all signed the three-page agreement and Oryx was expected to sign soon, the Ecuadorean industry source said.
PetroEcuador had asked the companies to pay for the entire project in return for use of 50 percent of the new capacity, but he said the companies were unlikely to accept this.
"It's a very elementary agreement... it is still possible that the five companies won't agree," he said. The first meeting for the group is scheduled for May 2.
One foreign oil executive in Ecuador said the scheme could be paid for by the foreign companies in the form of advance tariffs for using the line.
If the project goes ahead in its current form, oil exports could jump by up to 85,000 bpd within 12 months, analysts said.

Currently, Ecuador is withholding about 65,000 bpd production and some companies are planning to bring on new fields soon. City Investing plans to increase its output by 10,000 bpd this year while the Villano field, run by ARCO and Agip, is expected to start pumping 30,000 bpd in 1999.
